title: Capstone Operations: Record a Sale Transaction
learningObjectives: Describe the related writes required to record a sale.
Use a transaction to group order and stock changes.
Use a guarded stock update to avoid reducing stock below zero.
Verify that the sale and stock balance agree after commit.
Explain why production applications must handle concurrent stock requests.

understand.concept: Recording a sale requires related writes: create an order, insert its line items and reduce stock. These changes should be committed together so the database does not retain an order without its stock movement or a stock reduction without a sale.
understand.whyItMatters: A transaction protects inventory and sales records from partial updates when one step fails.
understand.analogy: A database capstone is like a complete shop workflow: records, rules, operations and reports must all work together.
understand.analogyLimit: The analogy does not model database isolation, concurrent workloads, deployment security or recovery guarantees.

explain.narrative:
## Sale workflow
A sale typically creates an order header, adds one or more order items, and reduces product stock. Each operation depends on the others.

## Transaction boundary
Start a transaction before the related writes. Validate stock availability, insert the order and items, update stock, and commit only if all required operations succeed. Otherwise roll back.

## Concurrency note
A production application must handle concurrent sales that compete for the same stock. Use guarded updates such as UPDATE ... WHERE stock_qty >= requested_quantity and check affected-row counts. The single-connection Playground does not simulate multiple concurrent clients.

### Correct transaction control
The guarded UPDATE is a useful concurrency-aware pattern because the availability condition is evaluated as part of the write. The application must check that exactly one row was updated before committing. If zero rows were updated, the application should roll back the earlier sale insert and report insufficient stock. If more than one row is possible, the key design is wrong and should be corrected.

### Concurrency boundary
A single-browser SQLite Playground session does not reproduce simultaneous sales from multiple application servers. Production systems need transaction isolation appropriate to the engine, proper constraints, retry handling for lock/serialization errors, and an affected-row check before COMMIT.

## Production application check
After the guarded stock UPDATE, inspect the affected-row count in the application. If it is not exactly one row for the intended product, ROLLBACK the sale instead of committing the order. The Playground example demonstrates the successful path; a single connection cannot simulate two sales racing for the same stock.

examples.title: Create stock and sales tables
examples.code: CREATE TABLE cap19_stock (product_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, stock_qty INTEGER NOT NULL CHECK (stock_qty >= 0)); CREATE TABLE cap19_sales (sale_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, product_id INTEGER NOT NULL, quantity INTEGER NOT NULL CHECK (quantity > 0));
examples.explanation: Creates a compact stock table and a sales table. The CHECK constraints reject negative stock values and non-positive sale quantities. This teaching schema omits a foreign key from sales.product_id to stock.product_id; a production schema should normally declare that relationship.

examples.title: Insert starting stock
examples.explanation: Inserts two starting stock balances. Product 1 has ten units and product 2 has five, establishing a known state for the transaction.

examples.title: Start a sale transaction and record a sale
examples.code: BEGIN; INSERT INTO cap19_sales VALUES (1, 1, 3); UPDATE cap19_stock SET stock_qty = stock_qty - 3 WHERE product_id = 1 AND stock_qty >= 3; COMMIT;
examples.explanation: Starts one transaction, records a sale for three units of product 1, then performs a guarded stock update that only matches when at least three units are available. With the supplied sample row, stock changes from 10 to 7. Critical limitation: plain SQL in this example does not automatically roll back the inserted sale when the guarded UPDATE affects zero rows. Application code must inspect the affected-row count and issue ROLLBACK instead of COMMIT if the update did not affect exactly one row.

examples.title: Verify the sale and remaining stock
examples.code: SELECT s.sale_id, s.quantity, st.stock_qty FROM cap19_sales AS s JOIN cap19_stock AS st ON st.product_id = s.product_id;
examples.explanation: Joins the sale to its current stock row using product_id. The result shows sale quantity 3 and remaining stock 7. In a full order model, join through a declared foreign key and include order/customer details as required.

examples.title: Check that stock is never negative
examples.code: SELECT COUNT(*) AS invalid_stock_rows FROM cap19_stock WHERE stock_qty < 0;
examples.explanation: Counts stock rows below zero. A zero result confirms that no negative quantity exists in this sample at query time; the CHECK constraint is the preventive control, while this SELECT is a diagnostic check.

practise.guidedTask: Run the sale workflow and verify that the sale quantity matches the stock reduction.
practise.independentTask: Create a transaction that records two order items and updates two product stock balances. Include a guarded update and describe how the application should roll back if one product has insufficient stock.
hints: Start the transaction before inserting related sale rows.
Use a WHERE condition to ensure enough stock exists.
Check the number of rows updated before committing in application code.
Commit only when every required step succeeds.
Handle concurrent sales with database transactions and affected-row checks.

questions.prompt: Why should sale and stock changes be in one transaction?
questions.explanation: A transaction keeps related sale and stock updates atomic.

questions.prompt: What does a guarded stock update do?
options: Updates stock only when enough quantity is available
questions.answer: Updates stock only when enough quantity is available
questions.explanation: The WHERE stock_qty >= quantity condition prevents an insufficient-stock update.

questions.prompt: When should the sale transaction commit?
options: After all required inserts and stock updates succeed
questions.answer: After all required inserts and stock updates succeed
questions.explanation: Commit only when all required business steps succeed.

questions.prompt: What should happen if one product has insufficient stock?
options: Roll back the entire sale operation
questions.answer: Roll back the entire sale operation
questions.explanation: A partial sale can leave order and stock data inconsistent.

questions.prompt: What does a single-connection Playground not simulate?
options: Concurrent clients competing for the same stock row
questions.answer: Concurrent clients competing for the same stock row
questions.explanation: Real concurrency requires multiple database connections.
